implementation_notes: The canonical Ruby/Rails mud is a set of ActiveRecord models that have accumulated callbacks, validations, scopes and business rules until no operation can happen without touching most of them, plus controllers that orchestrate several models directly. Diagnosis is available: `rails routes`, the `ActiveRecord::Base.descendants` list and a query count per request show the fan-out. Consolidation is what Rails' own `concerns`, service objects and form objects are for — but note the limit, since `concern` keeps the methods on the same class and only moves the file. `zeitwerk` autoloading means a mud's import cost is invisible until a production request touches a file for the first time.
idiom_name: Rails: fat models, fat controllers, callbacks and concerns everywhere
code_sketch:
# mud: one model owns the operation
class Order < ApplicationRecord
  after_save :charge_card, :sync_inventory, :notify, :audit
end

# consolidation: the operation has a name and a place
class Checkout
  def initialize(orders:, payments:, inventory:); end
  def call; end
end
pitfalls: `concern` reduces file size without reducing reach, which postpones the god object rather than removing it.
Rails' autoloading hides the import graph, so the cost of a mud surfaces as production latency on first touch rather than at boot.
A model with many callbacks is the Rails form of flag-driven control flow: the order of the callbacks is the control flow and it is not written down anywhere.
